pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — how people protect the ocean: marine protected areas (MPAs) limit fishing/pollution, sustainable fishing takes only what the ocean can replace, beach clean-ups reduce plastic, and international agreements cut carbon emissions that drive acidification.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y6 human impact on environments and how it can be reduced; citizenship/geography links to stewardship and choices.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-ESS3-1 and MS-ESS3-3 (design/evaluate methods for monitoring and minimising human impact on the environment) — solutions and their evaluation.
• Operational details: this is the SOLUTIONS partner to the harms topic. Core moves: explain what an MPA is and WHY it works (a refuge where populations recover and spill over); grasp SUSTAINABLE fishing as the renewable-resource idea — harvest at or below the replacement rate so the stock persists (over-harvest and it crashes); and name concrete actions across scales (personal plastic reduction → reserves → emissions treaties). There is a genuine trade-off/values dimension (fishing livelihoods vs conservation) worth surfacing, but the empirical core (yield vs replacement, MPA recovery) is quantitative and modelable.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): names ≥2 protective actions; Tier B (~10): explains what an MPA is and why it helps, and defines sustainable fishing as taking only what can be replaced; Tier C (~11): reasons about a trade-off (setting a catch limit / siting a reserve) balancing recovery against human needs.
bestPractices: Teach sustainable fishing as the renewable-resource principle: a stock replenishes itself, so harvesting at/below its replacement rate persists indefinitely while over-harvesting collapses it — make the replacement-rate idea explicit.
Show WHY MPAs work with a refuge-and-spillover model: protected populations grow and their offspring 'spill over' to replenish fished areas nearby.
Pair every solution with the problem it targets (from the harms topic) so protection is purposeful, not a list of virtuous acts.
Span scales of action — individual (reduce plastic), local/national (reserves, catch limits), international (emissions agreements) — so children see both personal agency and collective/policy levers.
Surface the real trade-offs (fishers' livelihoods, enforcement costs) and treat conservation as decision-making under competing needs, not a simple good-vs-bad story.
keyRepresentations: A fish-stock model: catch rate vs replacement rate (sustainable band vs collapse)
An MPA refuge-and-spillover diagram (protected core replenishing surrounding waters)
A scales-of-action ladder: personal → local → national → international
A problem→solution matching board linking each harm to its protective measure
commonMisconceptions: 'Sustainable fishing means stop fishing' — rather than harvesting within the stock's replacement rate.
'An MPA just fences off fish uselessly' — missing recovery and spillover that benefit surrounding waters too.
'One person recycling can't matter / only governments can act' — or the opposite, that personal acts alone are enough; missing the range of scales.
'Protecting the ocean has no costs or trade-offs' — ignoring livelihoods, enforcement and competing interests.
Thinking a depleted stock instantly refills once fishing stops — underestimating recovery time and thresholds.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of how people protect the ocean: marine protected areas (MPAs) as refuges where populations recover and 'spill over' to nearby fished waters; sustainable fishing as harvesting at or below a stock's replacement rate so it persists; and actions across scales (personal plastic reduction, local/national reserves and catch limits, international emissions agreements). The empirical core (yield vs replacement, MPA recovery/spillover) is quantitative and modelable; a genuine values trade-off (fishing livelihoods vs conservation) should be surfaced as decision-making, not a good-vs-bad story. Pair each protective action with the specific problem it targets.

activities.title: Manage the fishery: catch vs replacement and the reserve effect
feedback: If a high catch crashed the stock and income, highlight that you took more than the population could replace — like spending savings faster than any interest can refill them.
If lowering the catch stabilised the stock, name the threshold you found: catch at or below the replacement rate persists.
If the MPA rebuilt the core and lifted nearby catches, point to the spillover: big protected fish breed and their young move into fished waters.
If the depleted stock did not instantly refill after you cut fishing, note that recovery takes time and may need a population above a threshold to rebuild.
activities.rationale: The renewable-resource threshold and refuge/spillover are dynamic relationships that a learner can probe by setting catch limits and reserve size and watching the stock persist, crash or recover. A dual readout of fish population and fishers' income keeps the trade-off concrete rather than a slogan.
sourceClaims: Marine protected areas conserve habitats and allow fish populations to recover; sustainable fisheries management sets catch limits so stocks are harvested within their capacity to replenish.
learnerActions: Take charge of a struggling fishery with two controls: how much to catch each year, and how large a no-fishing marine protected area to set aside.
First try a high catch and track the fish population and the fishers' income over several seasons; record what happens when catch exceeds what the stock can replace.
Lower the annual catch to around the rate the stock replenishes and observe whether the population stabilises.
Set aside an MPA and watch across seasons whether the protected core rebuilds and whether young fish 'spill over' the boundary to raise catches nearby.
Write down, for each setting you tried, what happened to BOTH fish population and income, and state the catch/reserve combination that lasts.
activities.intendedInsight: A fish stock replenishes itself, so in this model, harvesting at or below its replacement rate can continue season after season, while over-harvesting that goes on shrinks the stock and can collapse it. How fast a stock replaces itself depends on how many fish are left, so a depleted stock refills slowly. A protected refuge lets fish grow and breed and, through spillover, can pay back the fishery it seems to close. Protection is not 'stop fishing everywhere' but fishing within what the ocean can renew.

activities.title: Negotiate a catch limit or reserve: whose needs?
feedback: If you ignored the fisher's livelihood, prompt: who bears the cost of this reserve now, and when might it pay back?
If you ignored recovery, prompt: will this catch limit let the stock replenish, or will it keep shrinking?
Credit answers that name a concrete trade-off and a timescale over which protection could benefit both sides.
activities.rationale: Who decides catch limits and whether a reserve is fair is a values and governance question well suited to speaking in role and articulating a stance. This is a proposed companion to the quantitative model, not a replacement for it; its efficacy is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Take a role in a negotiation to set a catch limit or site a reserve, speaking in turn as a fisher who needs income and a marine scientist who needs the stock to recover.
State each side's interest in your own words, then propose a catch limit or reserve boundary and justify it against both recovery and livelihoods.
Explain one cost of your chosen measure (lost fishing ground, enforcement, short-term income) and how it might pay back over time.
activities.intendedInsight: Protecting the ocean involves competing interests and real costs; good decisions weigh recovery against human needs rather than treating conservation as cost-free.

activities.title: Match each ocean problem to its protective action
feedback: If you said clean-ups alone will solve it, ask which problem they address and which (overfishing, acidification) they leave untouched.
If you treated the MPA as simply fencing off fish, point back to the core→spillover path that benefits surrounding waters.
If you said only governments (or only individuals) can act, show the ladder: agency exists at every scale and they work together.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-explore MPA/spillover diagram, a problem→solution board and a scales ladder present the mechanisms and vocabulary clearly; they are strong for exposition, though static diagrams cannot run the yield/recovery dynamics, so pair them with an interactive or hands-on model that can.
sourceClaims: Marine protected areas conserve habitats and allow fish populations to recover; sustainable fisheries management sets catch limits so stocks are harvested within their capacity to replenish.
learnerActions: Match each threat to a remedy that actually targets it: plastic litter → beach clean-ups and reducing plastic use; overfishing → reserves and catch limits; ocean acidification → cutting carbon emissions.
Explore a diagram of an MPA labelled with a protected core, a spillover zone, and a surrounding fished zone, and describe in your own words how the core helps the fished zone.
Place protective actions on a scales-of-action ladder: personal (reduce plastic) → local/national (reserves, catch limits) → international (emissions agreements).
Explain why cutting carbon emissions counts as ocean protection even though it is about the air (CO2 drives acidification), and name one ocean problem beach clean-ups do NOT fix.
activities.intendedInsight: Different threats need different, matched remedies acting at different scales; no single action fixes everything, and both personal and collective/policy levers matter.

activities.title: Check and defend the reasoning (diagnostic)
feedback: Full answer: explains that an MPA lets fish grow big and breed undisturbed, those larger fish produce far more young, and fish, eggs and larvae spill over into surrounding waters where people can fish — so protecting one area can raise nearby catches over time, working together with taking only what the ocean can replace.
If sustainability is defined as 'fishing carefully/nicely' or 'gentle gear', anchor it to the replacement rate: harvest at or below the rate the population regrows, like taking interest not savings.
If the fishery is treated as a fixed number to share, model a breeding population: leave some big fish to spawn and numbers rebuild and spill over; take them all and it crashes.
If one action is expected to fix everything, match each distinct threat to its distinct remedy.
activities.rationale: The 'how could it give MORE fish?' clause forces the replenishment idea into the open: a fixed-stock view has no way to answer it, discriminating conceptual understanding from vocabulary recall. A response format like this can be used during teaching as well as to check learning.
sourceClaims: Marine protected areas conserve habitats and allow fish populations to recover; sustainable fisheries management sets catch limits so stocks are harvested within their capacity to replenish.
learnerActions: Respond to this scenario: A town wants more fish for years to come, so a scientist suggests making part of the bay a marine protected area where NO fishing is allowed at all. A child objects: 'that's silly — if you stop fishing there you'll get FEWER fish to catch, not more.' Do you agree, and how could closing an area to fishing end up giving people MORE fish?
Explain how leaving big fish alone in a reserve could put MORE fish in the nets of boats fishing just outside it.
Define 'sustainable' precisely: what exactly has to be true about how much we take for fishing to go on forever?
Define what an MPA is and name at least two actions people can take to protect oceans.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who sees fish as a fixed stock to divide thinks any closed area means fewer fish; a learner who understands replenishment sees that protection lets breeding recover and spill over, which can raise nearby catches over time, especially where the stock had been overfished.

constraints: Make the replacement-rate idea explicit: a stock replenishes itself, so harvesting at/below replacement lets it persist, while continued over-harvesting shrinks it and can collapse it.
Pair every solution with the specific problem it targets so protection is purposeful rather than a list of virtuous acts.
Span scales of action (personal, local/national, international) so learners see both personal agency and collective/policy levers.
Surface real trade-offs (livelihoods, enforcement costs); treat conservation as decision-making under competing needs.
Account for recovery time: a depleted stock does not instantly refill when fishing stops, and rebuilding may need the population above a threshold.
Static diagrams and matching boards are scaffolds for mechanism and vocabulary; they present the ideas but cannot run the yield/recovery dynamics, so pair them with an interactive or hands-on model.
Recognition/matching tasks check vocabulary and pairing; they do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation of the replenishment mechanism, which needs constructed reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and both listed sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The negotiation activity's source attribution was cleared to [] because neither listed source directly supports the efficacy of role-play/dialogue for teaching the values trade-off; the NGSS claim concerns designing/evaluating methods, which is topic-adjacent rather than support for the dialogue principle.

The source row rated 3D as 'poor' with the claim it 'adds nothing'; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal law.

The 'take interest not the savings' analogy is a useful intuition but is an idealisation; real stock dynamics are nonlinear and replacement rate varies with population size and environment — present it as an approximation.

The source framed the interactive as uniquely able to make sustainability 'click'; this comparative/efficacy claim has been removed. The interactive is described only by the observable affordance that it can run the yield/recovery dynamics static media cannot, without claiming it is the only or best way to teach the concept.

probeDeeper: Explain how leaving big fish alone in a reserve could put MORE fish in the nets of boats fishing just outside it.
'Sustainable' — what exactly has to be true about how much we take for fishing to go on forever?
Beach clean-ups pick up plastic. Which ocean problems do they NOT fix, and what would?
Why might cutting carbon emissions count as protecting the ocean, even though it's about the air?
assess.correctAnswer: The child's objection is wrong. A marine protected area lets fish live, grow big and breed undisturbed; those larger fish produce far more young, and fish (and their eggs and larvae) spill over into the surrounding waters where people CAN fish. So protecting one area can raise catches nearby over time. This works together with sustainable fishing — taking only what the ocean can replace — so the population keeps refilling itself instead of being emptied.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Fish are a fixed amount — protecting some just leaves fewer to catch' — no notion of a breeding population that regrows.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model a breeding population: leave some big fish to spawn and the numbers rebuild and spill over; take them all and it crashes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — no fishing there means fewer fish for people, so a protected area just wastes good fishing ground.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the fishery as a set number to share out; can't explain how a closed area could increase the catch.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Sustainable fishing just means fishing carefully/nicely' — not 'taking only what can be replaced'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor it to the replacement idea: harvest at or below the rate the population regrows, like taking interest not the savings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Defines sustainable fishing as using gentle gear or not littering, with no idea of a replacement rate.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One big action (a clean-up / a ban) fixes the ocean' — single-solution thinking.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match each threat to its remedy (litter→clean-ups/less plastic; overfishing→reserves+quotas; acidification→cut CO2); no single action covers all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says beach clean-ups alone will solve it; doesn't connect protection, sustainable fishing and cutting emissions as needing to work together.

responseLevels.gap: Sees protection as pure loss (fewer fish); defines sustainability vaguely; expects one action to fix everything.
responseLevels.full: Explains how an MPA raises future catches via breeding and spillover, defines sustainable fishing as harvesting within the replacement rate, and matches distinct actions to distinct threats — transferring to judge a proposed measure.
responseLevels.partial: Can name protections (MPAs, sustainable fishing, clean-ups, emission cuts) but treats them as a list — can't explain the replenishment mechanism or match remedy to threat.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A town wants more fish for years to come, so a scientist suggests making part of the bay a marine protected area where NO fishing is allowed at all. A child objects: 'that's silly — if you stop fishing there you'll get FEWER fish to catch, not more'. Do you agree — and how could closing an area to fishing end up giving people MORE fish?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child thinking of fish as a fixed stock you divide up says any closed area means fewer fish overall; a child who understands populations replenish sees that protection lets breeding recover and spill over, raising the total. The 'how could it give MORE fish?' clause forces the replenishment idea into the open — a fixed-stock view has no way to answer it.
